San Ildefonso Pueblo

San Ildefonso is a distinct Tewa Pueblo whose public accounts connect community history, art and the Rio Grande landscape. Its preservation and environmental departments offer ways to study how cultural responsibilities and environmental work are organized.

Identity and context

San Ildefonso Pueblo is a living Pueblo nation in New Mexico.

Read the sources [1] San Ildefonso Pueblo

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Pueblo-authored history, Tewa language context, arts and community institutions. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] San Ildefonso Pueblo [2] San Ildefonso Pueblo

03

Community history and artists

The Pueblo’s visitor page relates an ancestral movement through Mesa Verde and Bandelier into the Rio Grande valley. It also credits Maria and Julian Martinez in its account of black-on-black pottery. This is an attributed Pueblo narrative; the guide has not independently reconstructed the full migration chronology or the artists’ careers.

Read the sources [1] San Ildefonso Pueblo

04

Preservation guided by the community

San Ildefonso’s THPO describes working with an advisory board and cultural authorities to guide preservation according to Pueblo values. Public responsibilities include outreach and identifying historically significant places. This explanation does not open private knowledge or sites to unrestricted access.

Read the sources [2] San Ildefonso Pueblo

05

Environmental work as an institution

The DECP traces its development through a 1992 accord, staffing and funding in 1996, and a move into a Natural Resources Building in 2002. It describes planning and risk assessment as foundations of its work. Those descriptions do not establish current environmental conditions.

Read the sources [3] San Ildefonso Pueblo

Visiting the Pueblo — attributed community history and arts ↗

The Pueblo presents its own historical narrative and credits Maria and Julian Martinez in black-on-black pottery. Attribution preserves the account’s perspective without independently resolving every chronology.
